title: Many words for love
hookLine: Greek philia and agape, Hebrew chesed, Arabic mahabba, Sanskrit bhakti: each with its own flavor

cards: English makes one word work very hard. The same love goes to a spouse, a grandmother, a best friend, a dog, a city, a song and a sandwich. Nobody's confused, exactly, but a lot gets packed into four letters.
Other languages, and the traditions that speak them, keep several words on the shelf, each with its own flavor.
So the love block opens with a handful of them, each from its own home, each naming something the others don't.

teach.b: First, two Greek words. Philia is the love of friends, the warmth of people who choose each other; Aristotle writes about it at length, and he's coming in a few days.
Agape is a word the New Testament uses for the love of God and of neighbor. The first letter of John says, "God is love," and the Greek word there is agape. Second, a Hebrew word.

Chesed is loyal, steady kindness, love that keeps its promises. The King James Bible renders it more than one way, often as mercy or lovingkindness. Psalm 136 repeats it again and again: "for his mercy endureth for ever."
Mahabba is love, and Sufi writers in Islam used it for the love between God and the seeker. The Qur'an speaks of a people whom God loves and who love Him. Fourth, a Sanskrit word.
Bhakti is devotion, love turned toward God.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water with devotion, he accepts it. They aren't five labels for one thing.
They're different loves, named by people who noticed something particular about each, and swap one for another and the flavor is lost.

how: Each tradition has its own vocabulary of love: Christians speak of agape, Jews of chesed, Sufi Muslims of mahabba, Hindus of bhakti, and the Greek philosophers of philia. Each is taught and practiced in its own setting.

o: a holy fear of God that keeps a person obedient
a burning, longing love for someone beautiful
loyal, steady kindness that keeps its promises

games.q: in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna speaks of what a devoted person can offer. what does he say he accepts?
o: even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, offered with devotion.
games.why: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. in bhakti, the devotion is what counts, not the size of the gift.

practice: Bring the loves in your life to mind one at a time and see which word fits: a friend you chose, maybe philia; someone you've stayed loyal to through hard years, maybe chesed; a plain wish for a stranger's good, maybe agape; a love reaching toward something larger, if you have one, maybe bhakti or mahabba.
There's no right answer, and no need to find every kind. Just notice how many loves are already there.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. A Hebrew word for loyal, steady kindness, one of four loves this lesson named, each with its own flavor. Today's word.
